analysis.one_liner: Lets workers redirect their Social Security payroll contributions into personal investment accounts with a guaranteed minimum benefit.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced in July 2004 with six Republican cosponsors, it was sent to a House subcommittee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let workers born in 1950 or later send most of their Social Security payroll contributions into personal investment accounts, similar to the retirement plan for federal employees. Money would go into conservative or stock-and-bond funds, and at retirement into an inflation-protected annuity. If a retiree's annuity fell short of the benefit they would have gotten under current law, the Treasury would pay the difference. Workers could opt out entirely, and leftover account savings could be spent or inherited.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born in 1950 or later who stayed in the program would own an account holding investments in their name, could pass what remained at death to heirs, and would pay no income tax on qualified retirement distributions. A federal guarantee backed by the Social Security trust fund would top up any annuity that fell below the promised benefit level.

how_it_helps.text: Participation was voluntary: any worker could renounce the program before retirement and stay entirely in traditional Social Security, and could later rejoin.

Account balances were defined as the property of the individual, and anything left after buying a retirement annuity would go to the person or, at death, to named beneficiaries or the estate — unlike traditional Social Security benefits, which largely end at death.

The bill guaranteed promised benefits: if a retiree's annuity paid less than the monthly amount due under the traditional formula, the Treasury would make up the difference from the Social Security trust fund.
Qualified distributions would be excluded from income tax, the accounts themselves would be tax-exempt, and death distributions would be excluded from the estate tax.

Investments were confined to broadly diversified stock-and-bond accounts modeled on the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, with the Board required to pursue low administrative costs and annual disclosure of fees.

analysis.who_pays: Because diverted contributions would no longer fund current retirees' benefits, the bill created a transition fund authorized to issue bonds, meaning the federal government would borrow to cover the gap. Participating workers would have their traditional monthly benefit reduced by an offset tied to the money moved into their accounts, and would bear market risk on that portion. Account administrative costs would be paid out of fund earnings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers via borrowing; workers via benefit offsets

drawbacks.text: A worker's guaranteed monthly benefit would be reduced by a formula tied to the contributions redirected into the personal account, so the traditional benefit floor would shrink for participants.

With contributions flowing out of the system, the plan would cover the shortfall by depositing trust fund surpluses into a transition fund and issuing Transition Fund Bonds — in effect borrowing against future budgets, on top of existing deficits.

Account values would rise and fall with markets: the default stock-and-bond account could hold up to 80 percent equities and self-directed options up to 85 percent, so workers retiring after a downturn could lock in losses.
Administrative expenses for the Board, asset managers, recordkeepers and annuity issuers would be paid out of the fund's investment earnings, reducing the returns credited to individual accounts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design tried to answer privatization's biggest objection by guaranteeing the promised benefit with Treasury payments and allowing opt-out, and the investment menu was deliberately narrow and diversified. But the transition was the weak point: keeping full benefits for current retirees while diverting contributions required new borrowing and assumed future budget surpluses and spending caps that Congress would have to maintain for decades. Critics of this approach note that workers would trade a guaranteed benefit for a market-exposed account whose offset against the traditional benefit is fixed regardless of how their investments actually performed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and then to the Social Security subcommittee, where it sat until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 with no markup, no floor vote, and no companion action.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Ryan (R-WI) introduced the bill on July 19, 2004, with original cosponsors Reps. Doolittle and Franks.
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and additionally to the Budget and Rules Committees.
Four days later, on July 23, 2004, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security, the standard step before any markup or vote.
No further action was taken; the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of Social Security privatization kept the existing guaranteed benefit system unchanged, and financial firms did not gain the new stream of payroll contributions into managed accounts. Workers' retirement protections were untouched — though they also gained nothing the bill's supporters promised.

for.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its personal-accounts redesign of Social Security.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Bill Thomas)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat in the Social Security subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; no recorded vote ever tested broader support.

industries.industry: Asset managers and mutual fund companies
industries.note: The bill would route redirected payroll contributions through Board-contracted asset managers and through Board-certified investment companies offering 'Tier III' options once an account passed roughly $7,000. That would create a huge new pool of worker retirement money earning management fees — paid out of the accounts' own investment earnings.

Retirees would be required to convert their accounts into Board-approved annuities with inflation protection, making certified insurers the mandatory sellers of every participant's retirement income. The requirement would guarantee insurers a captive market at retirement.
The bill required professional recordkeepers and custodians for the Tier I and Tier II funds, with costs paid from account earnings — steady fee income for back-office financial service firms.
